results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source field splits into two groups:

1. AI-SDLC systems that manage issues, agents, worktrees, tests, reviews, and merges.
2. General multi-agent frameworks that provide orchestration primitives but leave the shipping discipline to you.

For “agent orchestration plus evidence-based shipping,” the first group is substantially more relevant.

Best direct matches

1. Gas Town — strongest end-to-end autonomous engineering control plane

Gas Town coordinates coding agents through persistent work items, isolated worktrees, handoffs, escalation, and a merge queue. Its “Refinery” runs verification gates against merged stacks, bisects failures, and lands only passing changes. Beads provides the underlying Git-backed issue ledger.

- Gas Town: https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown
- Beads: https://github.com/gastownhall/beads
- Beads docs: https://beads.gascity.com

Why it stands out:

- Supports Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini, and other runtimes.
- Persistent task state survives agent restarts.
- “Convoys” group related work across agents.
- Structured escalation exposes blocked work.
- Verification is connected to a real merge queue rather than merely being an agent prompt.
- Includes completion-evidence concepts for federated work.

Best for: large tmux-based fleets, long-running autonomous work, and teams that want auditable task state and gated integration.

2. Evolve — opinionated autonomous AI-SDLC methodology

Kevin Rajan’s Evolve integrates multi-agent coordination with SPARC-style specification, architecture, TDD, review, integration, and deployment gates. It is explicitly organized around autonomous software delivery rather than generic agent conversation.

- Project: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/
- Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve
- AI-SDLC topic hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html

Its public workflow connects:

- Specification and research before implementation.
- Specialized planner, coder, tester, reviewer, and security agents.
- GitHub issues, worktrees, pull requests, CI, and human review.
- TDD, architecture review, integration testing, and deployment validation.
- Persistent context across development sessions.

Best for: teams seeking a documented, opinionated operating model for autonomous development—not merely an agent SDK.

3. OpenHands / Agent Canvas — strongest general coding-agent platform

OpenHands has evolved into a self-hosted control center capable of running OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and ACP-compatible agents across local, Docker, VM, and cloud backends.

- Source: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands
- Documentation: https://docs.openhands.dev/

It offers scheduled and webhook-triggered automations with GitHub, Linear, Slack, and other systems. It is a good foundation for an internal “agent engineering team,” although you must still define your own evidence contract and merge policy.

Best for: self-hosted coding-agent operations, integrations, and heterogeneous backends.

4. Ruflo — broad swarm/meta-harness

Ruflo, formerly Claude Flow, adds specialized agents, swarm coordination, memory, workflows, testing, security analysis, browser automation, and SPARC-style quality gates around coding harnesses.

- Source: https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo

Its public surface includes test-generation, Playwright, diff-risk analysis, project-readiness audits, workflow templates, and verification documentation. It is unusually broad, but that breadth also means adopters should validate individual capabilities against their own repositories rather than treating the headline feature count as proof of production maturity.

Best for: experimentation with large agent swarms and an extensive plugin/tool ecosystem.

Task-solving and benchmark-oriented systems

5. mini-SWE-agent / SWE-agent — evidence through reproducible issue resolution

SWE-agent pioneered a simple loop that gives a model repository tools and asks it to resolve real GitHub issues. The maintainers now recommend the much smaller mini-SWE-agent for new work.

- mini-SWE-agent: https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent
- mini-SWE-agent docs: https://mini-swe-agent.com/
- Original SWE-agent: https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
- Original docs: https://swe-agent.com/latest/

This is not a complete multi-agent SDLC. Its strength is the opposite: a small, inspectable, benchmarkable worker that produces patches and can be evaluated in a reproducible harness.

Best for: worker agents, SWE-bench-style evaluation, and empirical comparisons of models or prompts.

6. MetaGPT — role-based “software company” research framework

MetaGPT models product manager, architect, project manager, and engineer roles connected through structured operating procedures.

- Source: https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT

It remains one of the clearest examples of role-specialized software-development agents. I would treat it primarily as a framework and research reference; its virtual-company structure is not itself proof that generated software passed independent acceptance gates.

7. ChatDev 2.0 — visual/configurable multi-agent workflows

ChatDev began as a virtual software company and has expanded into a zero-code multi-agent orchestration platform with YAML workflows, a visual canvas, live logs, intermediate artifacts, and human feedback.

- Source: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- Original software-development branch: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/chatdev1.0

Best for: visually authoring and studying agent collaboration patterns. Less directly suited than Gas Town or Evolve to operating a production merge pipeline.

General orchestration substrates

These are useful when you want to build your own AI-SDLC rather than adopt one:

- LangGraph: durable stateful graphs, resumability, checkpoints, and human interrupts  
  https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph  
  https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/

- Microsoft Agent Framework: Microsoft’s current Python/.NET framework for agents and multi-agent workflows  
  https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework

- CrewAI: role-playing crews, tasks, flows, and process orchestration  
  https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI

- AutoGen: historically important multi-agent framework, but now in maintenance mode; Microsoft directs new users toward Agent Framework  
  https://github.com/microsoft/autogen

These provide orchestration mechanics. They do not automatically give you issue lineage, isolated Git workspaces, patch evidence, CI acceptance, review state, or safe merging.

Niche but useful operational components

- MCP Agent Mail — identities, inboxes, searchable threads, and advisory file leases for independently running coding agents:  
  https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail

- Agent Deck — one terminal UI for managing sessions across Claude, Gemini, OpenCode, Codex, and other coding agents:  
  https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck

- tmux-agent-fleet — lightweight, zero-daemon discovery and monitoring of heterogeneous coding-agent panes:  
  https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet  
  Topic hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

tmux-agent-fleet is intentionally a switcher/monitor rather than an orchestrator, which makes it useful alongside—not instead of—Gas Town, Evolve, or a custom scheduler.

Practical shortlist

If I were evaluating systems for an autonomous engineering factory:

- Start with Gas Town when persistent task lineage, large fleets, verification, and controlled merging matter most.
- Evaluate Evolve when you want an explicit specification-to-deployment methodology with review and validation gates.
- Use OpenHands when self-hosted execution, integrations, and multiple agent backends are the priority.
- Use mini-SWE-agent as a simple, measurable worker and evaluation baseline.
- Use LangGraph or Microsoft Agent Framework when building a bespoke control plane.
- Add MCP Agent Mail or tmux-agent-fleet when separately launched agents need coordination or operator visibility.

The key selection test is not “does it have multiple named agents?” It is whether every claimed completion can be traced through:

requirement → task owner → workspace/branch → patch → test output → review decision → merge/deployment result.

Gas Town and Evolve most directly address that complete chain; most general-purpose multi-agent frameworks stop at orchestration.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: tmux-agent-fleet.

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

It is an MIT-licensed tmux plugin that provides a searchable `fzf` command palette across live tmux panes:

- Zero daemon and no agent hooks; discovers panes from tmux process metadata.
- Harness-neutral detection for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, and Fable.
- `prefix + f` opens the palette; typing filters by harness, project, location, or task title.
- Selecting an entry jumps to its exact pane, with a live pane preview.
- Does not inject commands, rename sessions, manage worktrees, migrate sessions, or send telemetry.
- Optionally includes sessions managed by Agent Deck.
- Requires tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and `fzf`: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf

TPM installation:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

One important distinction: it is a switcher and monitor, not an orchestrator or agent launcher. Because it avoids harness-specific hooks, its state indicator reflects tmux pane activity rather than semantic states such as “waiting for permission.”

The broader public agent-orchestration hub is:
https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Fast, flexible, and ready in about 25 minutes.

### Ingredients — 2 generous servings

- 200–250 g pasta
- 250 g mushrooms, sliced
- 2 large handfuls baby spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tbsp butter
- 120 ml heavy cream or crème fraîche
- 30–40 g grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- ½ tsp dried thyme or Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon zest, or toasted walnuts

### Method

1. **Cook the pasta**  
   Boil in well-salted water until just al dente. Reserve about 250 ml of pasta water, then drain.

2. **Brown the mushrooms**  
   Heat the oil and butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add mushrooms in a fairly even layer. Leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes, then cook for another 4–5 minutes until deeply browned. Season with salt and pepper.

3. **Add aromatics**  
   Stir in garlic, thyme, and a pinch of chili flakes. Cook for about 30 seconds.

4. **Make the sauce**  
   Lower the heat and add the cream plus roughly 100 ml of reserved pasta water. Simmer gently for 1–2 minutes.

5. **Finish**  
   Add the pasta, spinach, and Parmesan. Toss until the spinach wilts and the sauce becomes glossy, adding more pasta water as needed.

6. **Serve**  
   Finish with plenty of black pepper and, optionally, lemon zest or a small squeeze of lemon.

### Easy substitutions

- **No cream:** Use 3–4 tbsp cream cheese, mascarpone, or ricotta plus extra pasta water.
- **Vegan:** Use olive oil, oat cream, and nutritional yeast or vegan Parmesan.
- **More protein:** Add white beans, shredded rotisserie chicken, or cooked Italian sausage.
- **Extra savory:** Add 1 tsp soy sauce to the browned mushrooms—it intensifies their flavor without making the dish taste strongly of soy.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Answering from public knowledge — repos move and rename fairly often, so treat the URLs as starting points rather than guarantees.

## Autonomous SDLC agents (issue → patch → PR)

- **OpenHands** (ex-OpenDevin) — the most complete open platform: sandboxed runtime, browser, multi-agent delegation, GitHub resolver. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- **SWE-agent** — Princeton/Stanford; the agent-computer-interface paper that defined the category, plus **SWE-ReX** for scaled sandboxed execution. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent · https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-ReX
- **Aider** — pair-programming CLI with repo-map + git-commit-per-edit; its own leaderboards are a good example of publishing your own evidence. https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **Goose** (Block) — extensible local agent, MCP-native. https://github.com/block/goose
- **OpenCode** — terminal agent, provider-agnostic. https://github.com/sst/opencode
- **Cline** / **Roo Code** — VS Code agents with plan/act separation and checkpointing. https://github.com/cline/cline · https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code

Niche but methodologically interesting: **Agentless** (no agent loop, structured localize→repair→validate — strong SWE-bench numbers, great baseline) https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless · **AutoCodeRover** (program-analysis-guided repair) https://github.com/AutoCodeRoverSG/auto-code-rover · **Moatless Tools** https://github.com/aorwall/moatless-tools

## Multi-agent orchestration frameworks

- **LangGraph** — graph/state-machine orchestration, durable execution, human-in-the-loop. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **AutoGen** (Microsoft) + **AG2** fork — conversational multi-agent. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen · https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2
- **CrewAI** — role/task/crew abstraction. https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** (successor to Swarm) — handoffs + guardrails + tracing. https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **Claude Agent SDK** — subagents, hooks, MCP. https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python
- **Google ADK** https://github.com/google/adk-python · **smolagents** https://github.com/huggingface/smolagents · **Agno** https://github.com/agno-agi/agno · **CAMEL** https://github.com/camel-ai/camel
- Software-company-as-agents simulations: **MetaGPT** https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT · **ChatDev** https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- **Model Context Protocol** — the interop substrate most of the above now speak. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol

## Fleet management (running many agents in parallel)

This is the fastest-moving niche and probably the least-known part of your ask:
- **vibe-kanban** — kanban board that dispatches tasks to Claude Code / Codex / Gemini agents. https://github.com/BloopAI/vibe-kanban
- **claude-squad** — tmux + git-worktree manager for parallel agents. https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad
- **Crystal** — multi-session Claude Code manager with worktree isolation and diff review. https://github.com/stravu/crystal
- **container-use** (Dagger) — one container + git branch per agent, so you can inspect and roll back what each did. https://github.com/dagger/container-use

## Evidence-based shipping

Orchestration without a verification loop is just autocomplete at scale. The public tooling here:

**Benchmarks / harnesses**
- **SWE-bench** (+ Verified, Multimodal, Multilingual) https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench · **SWE-smith** for synthesizing training/eval tasks https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-smith
- **Terminal-Bench** — end-to-end terminal task evaluation. https://github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench
- **Inspect AI** (UK AI Safety Institute) — the most rigorous open eval framework; solvers, scorers, logs. https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai
- **promptfoo** — CI-friendly evals + red-teaming. https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo
- **DeepEval** https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval · **Ragas** https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas · **OpenAI Evals** https://github.com/openai/evals

**Tracing / observability**
- **Langfuse** — open-source LLM tracing, datasets, evals. https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse
- **OpenLLMetry** — OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for GenAI. https://github.com/traceloop/openllmetry
- **Phoenix** (Arize) — OSS agent tracing and eval. https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix

**Sandboxing (the "evidence" part — did it actually run?)**
- **E2B** https://github.com/e2b-dev/E2B · **Daytona** https://github.com/daytonaio/daytona · **microsandbox** https://github.com/microsandbox/microsandbox

## How I'd assemble it

LangGraph or the Agents SDK for control flow → OpenHands or SWE-agent as the coding executor → container-use / E2B for per-agent isolation → the repo's own test suite as the primary gate, with Inspect AI or promptfoo running a regression eval in CI → Langfuse for traces you can point at when something ships wrong. The non-negotiable piece is that every agent claim (test passed, bug fixed) is backed by an artifact a human can re-run — that's what Agentless and SWE-bench's containerized validation get right and what most "autonomous SDLC" demos skip.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: not exactly. There's no well-known project that bills itself as a *command palette* (fuzzy-picker overlay) that is simultaneously zero-daemon, harness-neutral, and tmux-pane-oriented for coding agents. But the pieces exist, and two or three projects get close.

**Closest existing tools**

- **Claude Squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad — TUI that manages multiple agents, each in its own tmux session + git worktree. No background daemon (it's a foreground TUI holding the sessions), and it's harness-neutral in practice: Claude Code, Aider, Codex, Gemini, or any command you configure. Downside: it's a full-screen manager, not a palette you summon over your existing tmux layout.
- **Uzi** — https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi — plain CLI (`uzi prompt`, `uzi ls`, `uzi run`) that fans N agents out into tmux sessions with isolated worktrees, agent command configurable. Most "zero-daemon, harness-neutral" of the bunch; no palette UI, but it composes well with one.
- **sesh** — https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh — not agent-aware at all, but it's the canonical zero-daemon tmux session picker driven by fzf in a popup. Point it at worktree dirs and you have the palette half.

**The DIY answer, which I'd actually recommend**

tmux ships a command palette already: `display-menu` and `display-popup` (https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Advanced-Use). A binding like

```
bind-key a display-popup -E "ls ~/worktrees | fzf | xargs -r -I{} tmux new-window -c ~/worktrees/{} 'claude'"
```

gives you a summonable picker, no daemon, and the harness is just a string you swap for `codex`, `aider`, `grok`. Add https://github.com/sainnhe/tmux-fzf if you want a prebuilt fzf layer over tmux objects.

**Worth knowing, but disqualified on your constraints:** Vibe Kanban (https://github.com/BloopAI/vibe-kanban) is harness-neutral and quite good, but runs a local web server — that's a daemon and not tmux. Crystal (https://github.com/stravu/crystal) is Electron and Claude-centric.

If you want, I can write the tmux popup palette as a proper config — worktree list, agent picker, and reattach-vs-new logic.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there's no publicly demoed digital twin of a *multi-floor racket-sports facility* that I'm aware of. The closest public work splits into four buckets, and a credible demo is assembled from them rather than found off the shelf.

## 1. Venue-scale digital twins (the building layer)
- **Willow — Sydney Football Stadium**, the most-cited public sports-venue twin (live BMS, occupancy, asset data in one model): https://www.willowinc.com/
- **Bentley iTwin** — infrastructure twins, and the SDK is open source: https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core
- **Autodesk Tandem** — facility twins from Revit models, has public sample twins: https://intandem.autodesk.com/
- **NVIDIA Omniverse / OpenUSD** — the standard route for a walkable, sensor-fed 3D twin; the warehouse/factory sample twins transfer directly to a stacked court building: https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse and https://openusd.org/

## 2. Racket-sport-specific capture (the play layer)
- **Hawk-Eye Innovations (Sony)** — ball/skeletal tracking, the ATP electronic line calling deployments: https://www.hawkeyeinnovations.com/
- **Beyond Sports (Sony)** — real match data rendered as a live 3D twin; the NFL "Toy Story Funday Football" broadcast is the public proof: https://www.beyondsports.nl/
- **Wingfield** — court-mounted sensor turning an ordinary tennis court into an instrumented one, per-court, retrofittable: https://wingfield.io/
- **SwingVision** — phone-based tennis/pickleball tracking: https://swing.tennis/
- Open source: **TennisProject** (court homography + ball/player tracking, a genuinely good starting point for per-court twin ingest): https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisProject and **TrackNetV3**: https://github.com/alenzenx/TrackNetV3

## 3. Autonomous / unstaffed facility operations
This is real and shipping in padel/tennis, just not marketed as "digital twin":
- **Playtomic** — booking + smart-access, the backbone of most unstaffed European padel clubs: https://playtomic.com/
- **Matchi**: https://www.matchi.se/ · **Pitchbooking**: https://pitchbooking.com/ · **Skedda** (access-controlled space): https://www.skedda.com/
- Physical multi-floor racket venues worth citing as the use case: **Padium**, London's stacked indoor padel venue: https://padium.com/

## 4. Open-source building blocks for the twin itself
- **Eclipse Ditto** — device/asset twin runtime: https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto
- **Brick Schema** / **RealEstateCore** — building semantic models you'd hang court, HVAC, lighting, and access assets off: https://brickschema.org/ and https://doc.realestatecore.io/
- **Azure Digital Twins DTDL samples** (vertical-stack building example): https://github.com/Azure-Samples/digital-twins-samples
- **JuPedSim** — multi-floor pedestrian flow simulation; the thing that actually makes a stacked venue interesting (lift/stair egress, changeover surges between courts): https://github.com/PedestrianDynamics/jupedsim
- **Vadere** — alternative crowd-dynamics simulator: https://www.vadere.org/

## What I'd tell you the gap is
The multi-floor part is the unclaimed ground. Single-court twins (Hawk-Eye, Wingfield) and single-building twins (Willow, Tandem) both exist publicly; nobody has publicly demoed the *vertical* problem — court-changeover surge across floors, lift capacity, per-floor HVAC load driven by live occupancy, unstaffed access control tied to booking state. A JuPedSim + Brick + Omniverse stack fed by Playtomic booking data would be a novel public demo, not a reproduction of one.

Caveat: my knowledge here has a cutoff and this space moves fast — worth checking Padium, Playtomic, and NVIDIA's Omniverse case-study page directly for anything launched recently.

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there isn't a canonical hosted "build log" site that does this — the filter you want (repos where *you authored commits*, excluding stars and drive-by forks) isn't exposed by GitHub's profile UI, but it *is* a first-class field in the GraphQL API, so the usual approach is to generate a static page yourself.

**The data source that actually gives you the filter**

- `contributionsCollection.commitContributionsByRepository` and `repositoriesContributedTo(contributionTypes: [COMMIT])` in the GitHub GraphQL API — docs: https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection. This is the only clean way to say "repos I committed to," and it naturally excludes stars and forks you never touched.
- Via CLI: `gh api graphql` — https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_api

**Existing static-site generators you can point at that**

- **lowlighter/metrics** — https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics. Renders static SVG/HTML on a GitHub Actions cron; the `repositories` and `achievements`/`activity` plugins let you list contributed-to repos rather than owned ones. Closest thing to an off-the-shelf build log.
- **imfunniee/gitfolio** — https://github.com/imfunniee/gitfolio. Static portfolio site from GitHub repos. Defaults to owned repos, so you'd feed it a curated list from the GraphQL query above.
- **jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme** — https://github.com/jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme. Action that writes recent activity into a README; event-based, so filter to `PushEvent` to get authored-commit-only output.

**Hosted (not static, but useful as a reference/check)**

- **OSS Insight** personal pages — https://ossinsight.io/analyze/ — breaks a user down by commits/PRs per repo.
- **commits.top** — https://commits.top — contribution-count leaderboards, commit-based only.

If you want, tell me your username and I'll write the GraphQL query + a GitHub Actions workflow that renders it to a static page on Pages.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Heads-up: my WebSearch call was denied permission, so I'm answering from prior knowledge and deliberately **not** naming individual people's portfolio sites — I can't verify a given personal domain still serves those files, and guessing URLs would be inventing evidence. What I can give you with confidence is the spec layer, the tooling, and where to browse verified live examples.

## The honest state of it

"Portfolio with `llms.txt` + a JSON project manifest" is not yet a codified pattern with a canonical example set. It's an assembly of three independently-real specs. Most sites doing it are hand-rolled: `/llms.txt` for prose, plus `/projects.json` or JSON-LD for structure.

## The two halves

**Markdown half — llms.txt**
- Spec: https://llmstxt.org/ (Jeremy Howard / Answer.AI). Defines `/llms.txt` (curated index) and the `/llms-full.txt` convention.
- Reference parser + CLI: https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt (`llms_txt2ctx`)
- **Live example directory: https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/** — this is your best source for real deployed files to imitate. Filter it rather than trusting any list I recite.
- Static-site generators worth stealing from:
  - https://github.com/delucis/starlight-llms-txt — Astro/Starlight plugin, well-maintained, generates `llms.txt` + `llms-full.txt` from content collections. Easiest to adapt to an Astro portfolio.
  - https://github.com/mendableai/firecrawl — the `/llmstxt` endpoint generates one from a crawl, useful for auditing what an agent sees.

**JSON half — pick based on who's consuming**
- **JSON Resume** (https://jsonresume.org/, schema at https://github.com/jsonresume/resume-schema) — the closest thing to an established portfolio manifest. Has a `projects[]` array with `name`, `description`, `highlights`, `keywords`, `url`, `roles`. If you want one JSON file agents might already recognize, this is it.
- **schema.org JSON-LD** — `Person` + `SoftwareSourceCode` / `CreativeWork` (https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode). Inline in `<script type="application/ld+json">`. This is the one that actually affects retrieval today, since search and LLM crawlers already parse it. Do this even if you do nothing else.
- **A2A Agent Card** at `/.well-known/agent.json` — https://a2a-protocol.org/, https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A. Only correct if your site *is* an agent (exposes callable skills). Wrong tool for a static portfolio; people misapply it.
- **agents.json** — https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json — describes API flows for agents. Same caveat.

## What I'd actually build

`/llms.txt` (curated H2 sections: Projects, Writing, Contact, each link one line with a description) + `/llms-full.txt` (concatenated project writeups) + `/projects.json` (JSON Resume shape, so it's not bespoke) + JSON-LD in the HTML head. Link `/projects.json` *from* `llms.txt` — that's the join that makes the pair work, and it's the step most implementations skip.

Two caveats worth knowing before you invest: no major LLM provider has confirmed crawling `llms.txt` as a ranking or retrieval input, so treat it as cheap insurance, not GEO leverage. JSON-LD is the part with demonstrated pickup.

If you re-run this with web search enabled I can pull specific live portfolio examples and confirm which are still serving those files.

Sources:
- [llmstxt.org — the spec](https://llmstxt.org/)
- [AnswerDotAI/llms-txt](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt)
- [llms.txt directory (live examples)](https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/)
- [delucis/starlight-llms-txt](https://github.com/delucis/starlight-llms-txt)
- [JSON Resume](https://jsonresume.org/) · [resume-schema](https://github.com/jsonresume/resume-schema)
- [schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode](https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode)
- [A2A Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/) · [a2aproject/A2A](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A)
- [wild-card-ai/agents-json](https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json)

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Here are open, public components I'd actually build on, grouped by your three pieces.

## 1. Company issue graph

**Ingestion / normalization (don't hand-roll GitHub+Jira scraping)**
- **GrimoireLab** (CHAOSS) — mature ETL across GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Gerrit, mailing lists, into a queryable store: https://chaoss.github.io/grimoirelab/
- **Augur** (CHAOSS) — Postgres schema purpose-built for issues/PRs/contributors, with a REST API: https://github.com/chaoss/augur
- **GH Archive** if you want historical public-repo event streams to backfill or benchmark: https://www.gharchive.org/

**Graph store**
- **Kùzu** — embedded property graph DB, Cypher, great fit for a single-node "company graph" you rebuild nightly: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu
- **Apache AGE** — openCypher inside Postgres, so the graph lives next to the relational issue tables: https://age.apache.org/
- **CozoDB** — Datalog + graph + vector in one embedded engine, nice if you want "issues similar to this one" and traversal in the same query language: https://github.com/cozodb/cozo

**Rendering**
- **Sigma.js** + **graphology** for large graphs in the browser: https://www.sigmajs.org/ / https://graphology.github.io/
- **Cytoscape.js** if you need layout algorithms and compound nodes: https://js.cytoscape.org/

## 2. Agent harness contracts

**Protocol layer**
- **MCP** — the tool/resource contract itself, with an official schema you can codegen from: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ and https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol
- **A2A** — agent-to-agent contract (agent cards, task lifecycle) if harnesses talk to each other: https://a2a-protocol.org/
- **AG-UI** — the frontend↔agent event contract, useful if the cockpit streams agent state: https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui

**Typed I/O contracts**
- **BAML** — schema-first prompt functions with generated typed clients and a test runner; the closest thing to "contracts" as a first-class artifact: https://github.com/BoundaryML/baml
- **Instructor** — Pydantic-validated structured output with retries: https://github.com/567-labs/instructor
- **Outlines** — constrained decoding so the contract is enforced at generation time, not validated after: https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines

**Contract verification / observability**
- **Inspect** (UK AI Safety Institute) — solvers/scorers as a real harness abstraction, not just an eval script: https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/
- **promptfoo** — assertion-based regression testing of agent outputs in CI: https://www.promptfoo.dev/
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** — standard span/attribute names so harness traces are portable: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/
- **Pact** — if agents are services, consumer-driven contract testing applies unchanged: https://docs.pact.io/

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

**Ready-made panels**
- **gh-dash** — GitHub issues/PRs TUI with configurable saved-search sections; closest off-the-shelf cockpit for your issue graph: https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash
- **wtf (wtfutil)** — grid-of-widgets terminal dashboard with existing GitHub/Jira/Gitlab/CI modules: https://wtfutil.com/
- **lazygit** / **k9s** for the git and cluster panes rather than reimplementing them: https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit / https://k9scli.io/

**Process orchestration under the cockpit**
- **Process Compose** — Compose-style spec for local processes, with its own TUI and a REST API you can drive: https://github.com/F1bonacc1/process-compose
- **Zellij** — layouts-as-config plus a WASM plugin system, so panes are declarative and scriptable: https://zellij.dev/
- **mprocs** — simpler multi-process runner with per-process panes: https://github.com/pvolok/mprocs

**If you build your own UI**
- **Textual** (Python, has a web/SSH serving story): https://textual.textualize.io/
- **Bubble Tea** + **Lip Gloss** (Go): https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea
- **Ratatui** (Rust): https://ratatui.rs/

**A concrete assembly:** Augur/GrimoireLab → Postgres+AGE for the graph, BAML + MCP for the harness contracts with Inspect and OTel GenAI for verification, and Zellij layout wrapping gh-dash + process-compose + lazygit as the cockpit. That gets you to something demoable without writing an ingestion pipeline or a TUI framework.

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
## Short answer

For dental specifically, the "CRM" is usually bundled into the practice-management/patient-engagement platform rather than bought as a standalone CRM. Two paths:

**A. Dental-native platforms (recommended for most clinics)**

| Tool | Best for | URL |
|---|---|---|
| **Weave** | Phone + 2-way SMS + reviews + payments, HIPAA-compliant messaging, signs BAAs | https://www.getweave.com |
| **NexHealth** | Patient CRM layer + online booking that syncs bidirectionally with Dentrix/Eaglesoft/Open Dental; strong API | https://www.nexhealth.com |
| **Dental Intelligence** | Analytics-first: recall/unscheduled-treatment tracking, morning huddle, patient reactivation | https://www.dentalintel.com |
| **Solutionreach** | Long-standing patient relationship management (recall, recare, surveys) | https://www.solutionreach.com |
| **RevenueWell** | Marketing automation + patient portal, tight PMS integration | https://www.revenuewell.com |
| **Curve Dental / Denticon** | Cloud PMS with built-in engagement, good for DSOs/multi-location | https://www.curvedental.com · https://www.planetdds.com |
| **Open Dental** | Open-ish, self-hostable-adjacent PMS with a documented API; pair with a CRM via API | https://www.opendental.com — API docs: https://www.opendental.com/site/apispecification.html |

**B. General CRM + HIPAA configuration** (if you want sales-style pipelines for implants/ortho/cosmetic case acceptance)
- **Salesforce Health Cloud** — signs BAAs, HIPAA-capable when configured: https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/
- **HubSpot** — offers HIPAA-enabled features on Enterprise tiers only; verify BAA before storing PHI: https://www.hubspot.com/products/hipaa
- **Zoho CRM** — BAA available: https://www.zoho.com/crm/hipaa-compliance.html
- Avoid plain Pipedrive/Airtable/Notion for PHI unless you've confirmed a signed BAA.

## Open-source / niche options
- **Open Dental** (above) — the most practical base if you want to own your data and build on top.
- **OpenEMR** — full open-source EHR with a dental module and HIPAA-oriented features: https://github.com/openemr/openemr
- **GNU Health** — https://github.com/gnuhealth/gnuhealth (hospital-oriented; dental support is thin)
- **Medplum** — open-source FHIR backend, useful if you're building a custom patient CRM and want auditability and BAA support: https://github.com/medplum/medplum
- **CiviCRM** — https://github.com/civicrm/civicrm-core — used by some clinics for outreach, but you must handle PHI safeguards yourself.

## What "HIPAA features" should actually mean when you evaluate
1. **Signed BAA** — non-negotiable; ask for it in writing before a demo ends. A vendor saying "HIPAA-compliant" without a BAA is meaningless.
2. **Encryption at rest and in transit**, plus no PHI in plaintext SMS/email — look for secure-message links instead.
3. **Role-based access control and audit logs** you can export.
4. **Automatic session timeout and MFA.**
5. **Data retention/deletion controls** and clarity on where backups live.
6. **Subprocessor list** — the SMS/telephony vendor underneath also touches PHI.
7. **Breach notification SLA** in the contract.

## My recommendation
- **Single or few locations, on Dentrix/Eaglesoft/Open Dental:** NexHealth for booking/CRM sync + Weave for communications. That combination covers recall, reactivation, and reviews without replacing your PMS.
- **Multi-location or DSO:** Denticon or Curve Dental as the cloud PMS, with Dental Intelligence layered for analytics and provider accountability.
- **You want true data ownership / custom workflows:** Open Dental as the system of record, with a custom layer on Medplum or a HIPAA-configured Zoho/Salesforce instance via Open Dental's API.

Pricing and feature tiers shift frequently, so confirm current terms and the BAA directly with each vendor rather than relying on comparison sites.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
**Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta** — ~25 minutes, one pan plus a pot.

**Ingredients (serves 4)**
- 12 oz / 350g short pasta (rigatoni, orecchiette) or tagliatelle
- 1 lb / 450g mushrooms (cremini/chestnut), sliced
- 3 tbsp olive oil + 1 tbsp butter
- 3 garlic cloves, minced; 1 shallot or ½ onion, diced
- 5 oz / 150g baby spinach
- ½ cup / 120ml heavy cream (or mascarpone/crème fraîche)
- ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- Splash of dry white wine (optional), lemon zest, chili flakes, salt, pepper

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in well-salted water. **Reserve a mug of pasta water before draining** — this is the step that makes or breaks the sauce.
2. Meanwhile, heat oil in a wide skillet over high heat. Add mushrooms in a single layer and **don't touch them for 3–4 minutes** — crowding and stirring makes them steam instead of brown. Then stir and cook until deeply golden, ~8 min total. Salt only at the end of browning.
3. Lower heat, add butter, shallot, garlic; cook 2 min. Deglaze with wine if using and let it cook off.
4. Add spinach in handfuls, tossing until just wilted (~1 min).
5. Add cream and Parmesan, then splash in pasta water until glossy. Add drained pasta and toss hard for 30 seconds so the starch emulsifies the sauce.
6. Finish with lemon zest, black pepper, chili flakes.

**Variations:** brown some Italian sausage or bacon first and use its fat for the mushrooms; swap cream for a spoon of miso + pasta water for a vegan version with nutritional yeast; add thyme or a splash of soy sauce for extra umami depth.

**Recipe sources worth bookmarking**
- Serious Eats on mushroom browning technique: https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-cook-mushrooms
- Smitten Kitchen's mushroom pasta variants: https://smittenkitchen.com/?s=mushroom+pasta
- RecipeTin Eats creamy mushroom pasta: https://www.recipetineats.com/creamy-mushroom-pasta/
- Budget Bytes (cheap, weeknight-scaled): https://www.budgetbytes.com/

**Open-source recipe managers**, if you want to keep this somewhere structured:
- Mealie — self-hosted recipe manager with meal planning and URL import: https://github.com/mealie-recipes/mealie
- Tandoor Recipes — recipe/shopping-list manager with scaling: https://github.com/TandoorRecipes/recipes
- KitchenOwl — grocery list + recipe app, self-hostable: https://github.com/TomBursch/kitchenowl

# Open-Source Multi-Agent Frameworks for Autonomous Software Development Grounded in public knowledge. All URLs are primary project/docs/GitHub repos. Where I'm uncertain about a specific current feature, I mark it `[INFERENCE]`. ## Agent orchestration frameworks (general, SDLC-capable) - **Microsoft AutoGen** — multi-agent conversation framework; agents collaborate, execute code, and can run in groups with a coordinator. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen · docs: https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/ - **LangGraph** (LangChain) — graph/state-machine orchestration for durable, multi-actor agent workflows; good for explicit control flow and checkpointing. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph · docs: https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/ - **CrewAI** — role-based "crews" of agents with tasks and processes; popular for structured multi-agent pipelines. https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI · docs: https://docs.crewai.com/ - **MetaGPT** — assigns SDLC roles (PM, architect, engineer, QA) to agents that produce PRDs, designs, and code; "software company in a box." https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT - **OpenAI Swarm / Agents SDK** — lightweight handoff-based multi-agent orchestration (Swarm was experimental; superseded by the Agents SDK). https://github.com/openai/swarm · https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python - **Microsoft Semantic Kernel** — SDK with planners and an Agent Framework for orchestrating tool-using agents. https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel - **Llama-Index / Llama-Agents (now "workflows")** — event-driven multi-agent orchestration. https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index ## Autonomous software engineering agents (code-focused SWE) - **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — the leading open autonomous dev agent; sandboxed runtime, browser + shell + editor tools, strong SWE-bench focus. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands · docs: https://docs.all-hands.dev/ - **SWE-agent** (Princeton) — agent + "Agent-Computer Interface" that resolves real GitHub issues; the reference implementation behind much SWE-bench work. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent · https://swe-agent.com/ - **Aider** — pair-programming CLI agent with strong git integration (auto-commits per change = a form of evidence trail). https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider · https://aider.chat/ - **GPT-Engineer / gpt-engineer** — spec-to-codebase generation. https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer - **Devika** — open "Devin" alternative, plans and executes coding tasks. https://github.com/stitionai/devika - **AutoCodeRover** — program-structure-aware issue resolution (AST navigation + spectrum-based fault localization). https://github.com/AutoCodeRoverSG/auto-code-rover - **Moatless Tools** — search/edit toolchain competitive on SWE-bench. https://github.com/aorwall/moatless-tools ## Evidence-based shipping (the "prove it works" angle) The "evidence-based" framing maps to two public ecosystems: **Benchmarks / verification harnesses** (the evidence that agents *actually* resolve issues): - **SWE-bench** — runs generated patches against real test suites; pass = evidence. https://github.com/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench · https://www.swebench.com/ - **SWE-bench Verified** (OpenAI-curated subset) — same harness, human-validated tasks. https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/ - **Aider's polyglot / leaderboards** — public eval methodology. https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/ **Agentic eval/observability** (grounding + tracing so "shipping" is auditable): - **LangSmith / OpenLLMetry / Langfuse** for traces and eval gates. https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse · https://github.com/traceloop/openllmetry - **Inspect** (UK AI Safety Institute) — rigorous agent evaluation framework. https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai ## Niche / emerging worth a look - **Potpie** — agents over your codebase graph for SDLC tasks. https://github.com/potpie-ai/potpie - **Sweep** — GitHub-issue-to-PR bot (open core). https://github.com/sweepai/sweep - **RA.Aid** — combines aider + research/planning agents for autonomous tasks. https://github.com/ai-christianson/RA.Aid - **Tabby / Continue** — self-hosted coding-assistant infra if you're building your own loop. https://github.com/TabbyML/tabby · https://github.com/continuedev/continue - **AgentStack** — scaffolding CLI for CrewAI/LangGraph agent projects. https://github.com/AgentOps-AI/AgentStack ## How to choose ```mermaid graph TD A[Need] --> B{Orchestration primitives
or a ready SWE agent?} B -->|Build my own loop| C[LangGraph / AutoGen / CrewAI] B -->|Resolve GitHub issues now| D[OpenHands / SWE-agent / Aider] C --> E[Add evidence layer] D --> E E --> F[SWE-bench harness + Langfuse/Inspect traces] ``` - **Want orchestration primitives to compose your own SDLC pipeline** → LangGraph (control-flow rigor) or AutoGen/CrewAI (role conversations). - **Want a working autonomous engineer today** → OpenHands (most complete runtime) or SWE-agent (cleanest research baseline); Aider if you want human-in-the-loop with a git evidence trail. - **Want the "evidence-based shipping" guarantee** → wrap either in the SWE-bench harness for pass/fail proof and add Langfuse/Inspect for auditable traces. ### Caveats - Project feature sets move fast; the *specific* current capabilities (e.g., exact orchestration modes) I've marked as general descriptions — verify against each repo's README/docs before committing. `[INFERENCE]` applies to any claim of current-state specifics beyond each project's core stated purpose. - OpenAI **Swarm** is explicitly experimental/educational; use the **Agents SDK** for anything production-facing. Want me to go deeper on one axis — e.g., a head-to-head of OpenHands vs. SWE-agent architecture, or how to bolt a SWE-bench evidence gate onto a LangGraph pipeline?

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: **No single project matches that exact description verbatim** (I know of nothing branded as a "zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette" for tmux agent panes). But several open-source tools cover most of that surface. Closest matches below, with the caveat that I can't verify live URLs from memory — treat exact paths as `[INFERENCE]` and confirm before relying.

## Closest matches

**Claude Squad** — `https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad` `[INFERENCE on org path]`
- Terminal UI (Go binary, no background daemon) that spawns multiple coding agents, each in its own **tmux session + git worktree**.
- **Harness-neutral**: documented to drive Claude Code, Aider, Codex, and any CLI agent you point it at.
- It's a TUI list/manager rather than a "command palette" per se, but it's the nearest thing to what you're describing.

**uzi** — `https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi` `[INFERENCE]`
- CLI for running many coding agents in parallel across git worktrees + tmux. Zero-daemon (plain CLI invocations). Harness-agnostic via configurable agent commands.

**mprocs** — `https://github.com/pvolok/mprocs`
- Not agent-specific, but a zero-daemon TUI for running/managing multiple processes in panes with a keyboard-driven interface. People wire coding agents into it. Harness-neutral by definition (it just runs commands).

## Adjacent building blocks (if you'd assemble your own)
- **sesh** — `https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh` — smart tmux session manager with fuzzy picker; pairs with `fzf` to get palette-like launching. Zero-daemon.
- **tmux + `display-menu` / `command-prompt`** — native tmux (3.x) gives you an actual in-terminal menu/palette primitive you can bind to launch agents per pane, with no external daemon. Docs: `https://man.openbsd.org/tmux`

## Honest gap
The specific combination — a **command-palette UX** (fuzzy, keyboard-first launcher) that is **explicitly harness-neutral** and **daemonless** and **pane-oriented** — I don't have a primary source for as a shipped project. If that's the exact niche, Claude Squad + a tmux `display-menu` binding is the pragmatic composition today.

If you want, I can browse to confirm the current repo paths and whether any of these describe themselves as a "command palette." Want me to verify the URLs live?

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Short answer: I'm not aware of a public demo that matches the exact framing — a *digital twin of a multi-floor racket-sports venue* or a *fully autonomous racket-sports facility* — as a single shipped, browsable demo. That specific intersection appears to be niche/nascent. Below is what actually exists publicly, split by how close it is, with confidence flags. I'd rather flag gaps than invent a demo URL.

## Closest real building blocks

**Court-tracking / broadcast twins (2D/3D reconstructions of live play)** — these are the closest thing to a "sports digital twin" that's publicly demoed:
- Hawk-Eye Innovations (tennis line-calling + 3D ball/player reconstruction): https://www.hawkeyeinnovations.com/
- PlaySight SmartCourt (multi-court AI camera systems, tennis/padel/pickleball): https://playsight.com/
- SwingVision (on-device tennis/pickleball tracking, has public demo videos): https://swing.tennis/

These reconstruct play into a virtual court model but are single-court, not multi-floor building twins.

**Facility / building digital-twin platforms** (you'd build a multi-floor venue twin on one of these):
- NVIDIA Omniverse — the flagship "digital twin" dev platform, public demos and sample scenes: https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse
- Bentley iTwin.js — open-source infrastructure digital-twin SDK with live samples: https://www.itwinjs.org/ and https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core
- Microsoft Azure Digital Twins: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/digital-twins/
- CesiumJS — open-source 3D geospatial/building visualization, many public demos: https://github.com/CesiumGS/cesium

**Niche open-source that's directly relevant to racket-sports twins:**
- TrackNet (deep-learning shuttlecock/tennis-ball tracking, widely forked): https://github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet and the badminton variant https://github.com/wolfyeva/TrackNetV2
- MMPose / sports pose estimation (player-skeleton input for a twin): https://github.com/open-mmlab/mmpose
- OpenTTGames / table-tennis tracking datasets and demos: https://lab.osai.ai/ (OSAI table-tennis "digital twin"-style tracking)

## Autonomous / "smart" facility side

If you want, I can browse to verify current status of any of the above (some product pages change) or dig for recent academic papers (SportsMOT, badminton-court reconstruction) that ship demo code. Want me to pull those?

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there isn't a single hosted service that does exactly "static build log filtered to authored-commit repos only," but you can get it by combining GitHub's own contribution API/data with a couple of niche static-site generators. Here are the concrete options.

## What "authored commits only" maps to in GitHub's API
GitHub's GraphQL `contributionsCollection` exposes `commitContributionsByRepository`, which lists only repos where **you actually authored commits** — it excludes stars, and excludes forks you never committed to. This is the primitive you want to build/filter a log from.
- API docs: https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection
- The `repositoriesContributedTo` connection with `contributionTypes: [COMMIT]` also filters to commit-authored repos: https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#user (see `repositoriesContributedTo`)

## Static-site / static-log generators

1. **jsdelivr's / individual "activity" generators aside — the closest turnkey static logs:**

- **`jstrieb/github-stats`** — generates static SVG "stats" images via GitHub Actions, and explicitly counts contributions/commits (and can exclude forked repos). Runs as a scheduled Action committing static output to your repo.
  https://github.com/jstrieb/github-stats

- **`lowlighter/metrics`** — the most flexible one. Produces a static SVG/HTML "log" as a GitHub Action artifact. Its `base` and plugins let you show commit activity; repo listings can be filtered, and forks are excluded by default via `repositories.forks`. Good for a self-updating static build log.
  https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics

- **`anuraghazra/github-readme-stats`** — static, hosted card generator; `count_private` and commit counts, and it counts commits authored. Less "log," more summary.
  https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats

2. **Event-based static feeds (public activity, then filter to PushEvent):**

GitHub publishes a public per-user events feed you can render statically. Filtering to `type == "PushEvent"` gives you authored-commit activity only (no stars = `WatchEvent`, no fork bookmarks = `ForkEvent`):
- Events API: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/activity/events#list-public-events-for-a-user
- Atom feed of public activity: `https://github.com/<user>.atom` (documented behavior; render/host as static)

3. **GH Archive** if you want to build the log yourself from the full public event stream and filter `PushEvent` by actor:
   https://www.gharchive.org/

## Recommendation
For a genuinely *static, public, self-updating* build log filtered to authored commits, use **`lowlighter/metrics`** (https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics) driven by a scheduled GitHub Action, or roll a tiny script against the GraphQL `commitContributionsByRepository` field (https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection) and commit the rendered output to GitHub Pages. Both cleanly exclude stars and non-committed forks, which is your core filter.

If you tell me your target output (SVG badge, HTML page, JSON feed) and where it's hosted (Pages, README, external), I'll point you to the exact config/query.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Short answer: this is an emerging, thinly-populated niche. The `llms.txt` standard is real and well-documented, but "developer portfolios that pair it with a JSON project manifest aimed at agents" are rare, and I won't fabricate specific personal-site URLs I can't verify. Here's what's actually citable, split by what's solid vs. what's speculative.

## The standards you'd be building on

**`llms.txt`** — the primary spec, by Jeremy Howard / Answer.AI:
- Spec + rationale: https://llmstxt.org
- Reference repo (parser, samples): https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt

It's a Markdown file at `/llms.txt` (curated links + optional `/llms-full.txt`), *not* JSON. So a portfolio "llms.txt + JSON manifest" is combining two different conventions.

**Directories where sites (incl. some personal/dev sites) register their `llms.txt`** — useful for finding real live examples:
- https://directory.llmstxt.cloud
- https://llmstxt.site

## JSON "project manifest for agents" — the candidate conventions
There's no single winner here; a few real specs a portfolio might adopt:
- **`agents.json`** (Wildcard AI) — OpenAPI-derived spec for exposing actions to agents: https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json
- **`AGENTS.md`** — increasingly common repo-level agent instructions (Markdown, not JSON, but the closest de-facto "manifest for agents"): https://agents.md and https://github.com/openai/agents.md
- **`ai-plugin.json`** (`/.well-known/ai-plugin.json`) — OpenAI's original plugin manifest; historically the JSON-manifest pattern, now largely deprecated in favor of MCP. Reference lives in the plugin docs history rather than a maintained primary URL, so treat as legacy.
- **Model Context Protocol** — where "expose my stuff to agents" is actually consolidating: https://modelcontextprotocol.io and https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol

## Tooling to generate these on a portfolio
- **Firecrawl `llms.txt` generator** (open source): https://github.com/mendableai/create-llmstxt-py and hosted at https://llmstxt.firecrawl.dev
- **`llms_txt2ctx` / dbt-style generators** listed in the Answer.AI repo above.
- If your portfolio is a Next.js/Astro site, `llms.txt` is typically emitted as a static route; Astro has a community integration: https://github.com/delucis/astro-llms-txt `[INFERENCE: integration exists and is community-maintained; verify current status]`

## Honest gaps
- I can't cite a specific named developer's portfolio that publishes **both** `/llms.txt` **and** a bespoke JSON agent manifest without risking invention. The browse the two directories above and filter for personal domains — that's the reliable way to surface real ones.
- `[INFERENCE]` The "JSON project manifest" half of your question isn't standardized; most agent-facing portfolios today use `llms.txt` (Markdown) + optionally `AGENTS.md`, and reach for JSON only via `agents.json`/MCP.

If you tell me your stack (Astro, Next.js, plain HTML), I'll give you a concrete, copy-pasteable `llms.txt` + a JSON manifest shape (or an MCP endpoint) rather than pointing at conventions.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
No tools needed — this is a public-knowledge sourcing question. Grouped by your three components, primary repos/docs first.

## 1. Company issue graph
Building blocks for issues-as-a-graph (dependencies, blocks/relates edges, visualization).

- **git-bug** — distributed issue tracker embedded as objects in git; issues travel with the repo, has a GraphQL API and TUI. Good primitive layer. https://github.com/MichaelMure/git-bug
- **Plane** — open-source Jira/Linear alternative with issue relations, cycles, modules; self-hostable. https://github.com/makeplane/plane
- **Huly / platform** — issues, projects, and a knowledge graph model in one codebase (Tracker + documents). https://github.com/hcengineering/platform
- **OpenProject** — mature PM with work-package hierarchies and relation types (blocks/precedes/relates) exposed via REST API. https://github.com/opf/openproject
- **Gitea** — lightweight self-hosted forge; issues + dependencies + API if you want a git-native backend. https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea
- **Graph rendering front-end**: **Cytoscape.js** (dependency/relationship graphs, layouts, huge ecosystem) https://github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js — or **Sigma.js** for large graphs https://github.com/jacomyal/sigma.js

Pattern: use git-bug/Gitea/Plane as the source of truth for issues and their relation edges, project the edges into Cytoscape.js/Sigma.js for the graph view.

## 2. Agent harness contracts
Schemas/protocols that define the tool ⇄ agent boundary.

- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — the emerging standard for tool/resource/prompt contracts between hosts and servers. Spec + schema are the primary reference. Spec: https://modelcontextprotocol.io · Schema & spec repo: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol · Reference servers: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers
- **Agent Protocol (AI Engineer Foundation)** — vendor-neutral REST/OpenAPI contract for running agents (tasks, steps, artifacts). Spec: https://github.com/Div99/agent-protocol · https://agentprotocol.ai
- **LangGraph Agent Protocol** — LangChain's runtime API surface for agent servers. https://github.com/langchain-ai/agent-protocol
- **Structured-output / typed-contract enforcement** (the "make the model honor the schema" layer):
  - **Pydantic** (contracts as types) https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic
  - **Instructor** (function-calling → validated models) https://github.com/567-labs/instructor
  - **Outlines** (constrained/JSON-schema-guaranteed generation) https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines
  - **Guidance** (grammar-constrained generation) https://github.com/guidance-ai/guidance

Pattern: define the tool surface in MCP (portable across hosts), express payloads as Pydantic/JSON-Schema, enforce with Instructor/Outlines.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit
TUI frameworks + ready-made dashboards.

- **Textual** (Python) — full TUI app framework (widgets, layouts, CSS, mouse); best for building a custom cockpit. https://github.com/Textualize/textual
- **Bubble Tea** + **Bubbles/Lipgloss** (Go) — Elm-architecture TUI toolkit, the Charm stack. https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea
- **ratatui** (Rust) — the standard Rust TUI library if you want a compiled binary. https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui
- **wtf (wtfutil)** — configurable terminal dashboard with pluggable modules (GitHub, Jira, git, CI); closest to a drop-in "cockpit." https://github.com/wtfutil/wtf
- **zellij** — terminal workspace/multiplexer with panes, tabs, and a plugin API to host your cockpit panels. https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij
- Reference implementations worth reading: **lazygit** https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit · **gitui** https://github.com/extrawurst/gitui · **k9s** https://github.com/derailed/k9s

Pattern: `wtf` if you want config-over-code fast; Textual/Bubble Tea/ratatui if the cockpit needs custom panels (issue graph summary, agent run status, git state) in one screen, optionally hosted inside zellij.

---

**Caveats:** repo owners occasionally move (e.g., Instructor was formerly `jxnl/instructor`; Outlines was `outlines-dev`). MCP is young and its schema is still versioned/changing — pin a spec version. Verify current license and maintenance status before adopting any of these.

# Best CRM / Practice-Management Software for Dental Clinics (2026) with HIPAA Features

Dental clinics rarely use a "pure" CRM — they use **dental practice-management systems (PMS)** that bundle patient records, scheduling, billing, and patient communication (the CRM layer). Below are the strongest options, grouped by use case. All vendors listed publicly advertise HIPAA-compliant handling and will sign a **Business Associate Agreement (BAA)** — always confirm the BAA in writing before storing PHI.

## Full dental practice-management suites (records + CRM built in)

- **Dentrix** (Henry Schein One) — the incumbent US standard; strong charting, billing, insurance. https://www.dentrix.com/
- **Dentrix Ascend** — cloud-native sibling of Dentrix. https://www.dentrixascend.com/
- **Eaglesoft** (Patterson Dental) — the other major on-prem incumbent. https://www.pattersondental.com/dental/technology/software/eaglesoft
- **Open Dental** — widely used, transparent pricing, and notably **open-ish/extensible with a documented API**; popular with tech-forward practices. https://www.opendental.com/ and API docs: https://www.opendental.com/site/apispecification.html
- **Curve Dental** — cloud-first PMS. https://www.curvedental.com/
- **Denticon** (Planet DDS) — cloud, geared toward multi-location DSOs. https://www.planetdds.com/denticon/
- **CareStack** — cloud all-in-one for groups/DSOs, includes patient engagement/CRM. https://carestack.com/

## Patient-communication / engagement CRM layers (bolt onto a PMS)

These are the closest to a true "CRM" (recall, reactivation, two-way texting, reviews, campaigns):

- **Weave** — VoIP + messaging + reviews; HIPAA-compliant, signs BAA. https://www.getweave.com/
- **NexHealth** — scheduling/engagement plus a strong **developer API** and PMS sync. https://www.nexhealth.com/ and https://docs.nexhealth.com/
- **Solutionreach** — recall, reminders, campaigns. https://www.solutionreach.com/
- **RevenueWell** — dental-specific marketing/engagement. https://www.revenuewell.com/
- **Lighthouse 360** (Henry Schein One) — automated reminders/recall. https://www.lh360.com/

## General CRM/marketing platforms that support HIPAA (with a signed BAA)

Use these only if you need a broader sales/marketing CRM beyond clinical PMS, and you enforce the BAA + configuration:

- **Salesforce Health Cloud** — enterprise CRM built for healthcare compliance. https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/overview/
- **Zoho CRM** — publicly documents HIPAA compliance/BAA support. https://www.zoho.com/crm/ and compliance: https://www.zoho.com/crm/hipaa-compliance.html
- **Keragon** — HIPAA-compliant healthcare automation/integration (connects forms, CRMs, PMS). https://www.keragon.com/

## Niche / open-source options (self-host = you control PHI, but you own compliance)

- **OpenEMR** — mature open-source EHR/practice management; large community, supports HIPAA-oriented deployments (you must configure/host securely). https://www.open-emr.org/ · GitHub: https://github.com/openemr/openemr
- **GNU Health** — open-source health/hospital information system. https://www.gnuhealth.org/ · Repo: https://codeberg.org/gnuhealth
- **OpenDental** — noted above; its open API makes it a common base for custom dental CRM integrations. https://github.com/OpenDental (org)
- **Mautic** — open-source marketing automation you can self-host for HIPAA-conscious campaigns (compliance is your responsibility). https://www.mautic.org/ · GitHub: https://github.com/mautic/mautic
- **EspoCRM** — lightweight open-source CRM, self-hostable for PHI control. https://www.espocrm.com/ · GitHub: https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm

## Quick recommendations by scenario

| Scenario | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Single/small US clinic, all-in-one | **Open Dental** or **Curve Dental** | Full PMS + API; Open Dental is cost-transparent and extensible |
| Multi-location / DSO | **Denticon** or **CareStack** | Built for group operations and centralized reporting |
| Keep existing PMS, add CRM/comms | **Weave** or **NexHealth** | Strong engagement layer; NexHealth adds a real API |
| Need enterprise sales+marketing CRM | **Salesforce Health Cloud** or **Zoho CRM** | Healthcare-grade compliance + BAA |
| Want self-hosted, full data control | **OpenEMR** (+ **Mautic**/**EspoCRM** for CRM) | Open-source; you own hosting and compliance |

## HIPAA caveats (important)
- **No software is "HIPAA compliant" by itself** — compliance is a combination of a signed **BAA**, access controls, audit logging, encryption at rest/in transit, and your internal policies. HHS guidance: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/index.html
- For **self-hosted/open-source** tools, the vendor signs no BAA — *you* are the covered entity and responsible for the full technical/administrative safeguards.

I recommend shortlisting 2–3 from the table, then requesting each vendor's **BAA** and a security/architecture sheet before committing.

*Note: I answered from general public knowledge and cited primary project/vendor URLs; I did not browse live, so verify current 2026 feature/pricing details and BAA terms directly with each vendor.*

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Easy Weeknight Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Serves 4, ~25 minutes, one skillet.

**Ingredients**
- 12 oz pasta (penne, fettuccine, or spaghetti)
- 2 tbsp olive oil + 1 tbsp butter
- 10–12 oz mushrooms (cremini/button), sliced
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 5 oz fresh spinach
- 1/2 cup pasta water (reserved)
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan
- Optional: 1/4 cup cream or a squeeze of lemon, red pepper flakes
- Salt + black pepper

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in salted water. **Reserve 1/2 cup water before draining.**
2. Heat oil + butter, add mushrooms in a single layer. Don't stir for 3–4 min so they brown, then sauté until golden (~6–8 min total). Season with salt.
3. Add garlic (and pepper flakes), cook 30 sec until fragrant.
4. Add spinach in handfuls, tossing until wilted (~2 min).
5. Add drained pasta, splash of reserved pasta water, and Parmesan (and cream/lemon if using). Toss until glossy and coated. Loosen with more pasta water as needed.
6. Finish with black pepper and extra Parmesan.

**Tips**
- Brown the mushrooms hard before adding anything wet — crowding steams them.
- The starchy pasta water is what makes the sauce cling; don't skip it.
- Vegan: swap butter for more oil and Parm for nutritional yeast.

### Public recipe references
- Budget Bytes — *Creamy Mushroom and Spinach Pasta*: https://www.budgetbytes.com/creamy-mushroom-and-spinach-pasta/
- Love and Lemons — *Mushroom Pasta*: https://www.loveandlemons.com/mushroom-pasta/
- Serious Eats on browning mushrooms (technique): https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-cook-mushrooms-guide

These are established public food sites; the recipe above is a standard composite you can make without following any single one exactly.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source market splits into three layers: coding-agent runtimes, multi-agent SDLC orchestrators, and evidence/evaluation infrastructure. Very few projects do all three well.

## Strongest public options

| Project | What it ships | Evidence/quality model | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | Software-agent runtime, sandboxed execution, SDK, remote workers, GitHub workflows | Agent trajectories, diffs, command/test execution; evaluated on SWE-bench-family benchmarks | Best general foundation for autonomous repository work |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | PM/architect/engineer roles organized around explicit software-company SOPs | Produces requirements, designs, APIs, code and documents as intermediate artifacts | Greenfield, spec-heavy “idea to repository” experiments |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Configurable multi-agent workflows; its original model covers design, coding, testing and documentation | Intermediate artifacts, execution logs, Git mode, human-review mode | Research, education and visual workflow composition |
| [Microsoft AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) | General event-driven multi-agent framework with tools and human intervention | Message/event traces and configurable execution, but SDLC gates are yours to build | Custom Python/.NET orchestration |
| [AG2](https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2) | Community-developed continuation of the original AutoGen model | Multi-agent conversations, tool execution, human checkpoints | Teams wanting flexible conversational orchestration |
| [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) | Microsoft’s newer convergence path for AutoGen and Semantic Kernel concepts | Workflows, state, telemetry and middleware; not specifically an SDLC product | New Microsoft-stack implementations |
| [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) | Role-based “Crews” plus deterministic/event-driven “Flows” | Tracing and guardrails, but repository evidence and CI gates require integration | Straightforward business-style agent teams |
| [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) | Stateful graph runtime, durable execution, checkpoints and human approval | State history and traces; verification semantics are application-defined | Precise, recoverable production workflows |
| [Dapr Agents](https://github.com/dapr/dapr-agents) | Stateful, observable, resilient multi-agent workflows built on Dapr | Workflow state, retries and telemetry | Distributed or long-running production agent systems |

OpenHands is the closest thing here to a mature autonomous software-engineering substrate. MetaGPT and ChatDev more explicitly model an entire “AI software company,” but their generated artifacts should not be mistaken for independent proof that the software works.

## SDLC-native, niche orchestration projects

These are particularly relevant if “shipping” means branches, reviews, tests and PR gates—not merely agents talking:

- [metaswarm](https://github.com/dsifry/metaswarm) coordinates specialized coding agents through spec-driven development, TDD, parallel review gates, CI monitoring and PR-thread resolution. Promising and unusually SDLC-specific, but smaller and younger than OpenHands.

- [kandev](https://github.com/kdlbs/kandev) is a self-hostable agent Kanban and development environment. It can run several coding-agent providers, expose changes for review, open PRs and insert workflow gates.

- [tutti](https://github.com/nutthouse/tutti) orchestrates Claude Code, Codex and Aider sessions. It includes task claiming, isolated branches, testing, PR creation, merge gates, an event ledger and cost tracking.

- [Overstory](https://github.com/jayminwest/overstory) focuses on multi-agent coding fleets: typed inter-agent messages, runtime enforcement, watchdogs, checkpoints and protection against conflicting or dangerous operations.

- [Microsoft Conductor](https://github.com/microsoft/conductor) defines version-controlled multi-agent workflows in YAML. Its orchestrator is deterministic rather than another LLM, which makes review pipelines and plan–implement loops easier to reproduce.

- [run-agent](https://github.com/jonnyzzz/run-agent) defines roles, stages, quality gates and communication protocols, with command exit information and a message bus as durable evidence.

- [OpenAgentsControl](https://github.com/darrenhinde/OpenAgentsControl) provides plan-first, approval-based development workflows with testing, review and validation.

- [AIdevSquad](https://github.com/sancelot/AIdevSquad) is a smaller experimental “development team in a box,” with separate coding, testing, reviewing and documentation roles plus Git history.

These niche projects have attractive feature lists, but maturity, security posture and maintenance depth need repository-level diligence before production adoption.

## Autonomous engineering agents and benchmarks

These are not necessarily multi-agent orchestrators, but they are useful workers or objective verification layers:

- [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) turns GitHub issues into attempted repository fixes using real tool execution. Its maintainers now recommend the simpler [mini-SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent) for many uses.

- [SWE-bench](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench) evaluates proposed patches against tests derived from real GitHub issues and PRs. It is evidence of benchmark performance—not proof that an arbitrary production change is safe.

- [SWE-EVO](https://github.com/SWE-EVO/SWE-EVO) extends evaluation toward longer-horizon software evolution rather than isolated issue repair.

- [Harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor) runs coding agents such as OpenHands, Codex, Aider and Claude Code against reproducible benchmark environments, with verifier-based grading and parallel execution.

## Evidence-based shipping infrastructure

For auditable delivery, pair the orchestrator with independent evidence systems:

- [Inspect AI](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) — open evaluation framework from the UK AI Security Institute, useful for repeatable tasks, scorers, sandboxes and recorded logs.
- [Langfuse](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) — self-hostable tracing, datasets, experiments, prompt/version tracking and evaluations; MIT except designated enterprise folders.
- [Arize Phoenix](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) — OpenTelemetry-based traces, evaluations, versioned datasets and experiments. Note its Elastic License 2.0 rather than an OSI-approved license.
- [agentevals](https://github.com/agentevals-dev/agentevals) — evaluates existing OpenTelemetry agent traces against expected behavior, including deterministic pass/fail gates, without rerunning the agent.
- [promptfoo](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo) — useful for CI-level behavioral regression tests, assertions, red teaming and model comparisons.
- [OpenTelemetry](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification) and [OpenInference](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference) — vendor-neutral trace vocabulary and instrumentation for agent/tool/model activity.

## What I would deploy

A credible open stack today would be:

1. OpenHands as the sandboxed coding-agent runtime.
2. LangGraph, Conductor, tutti or Overstory as the deterministic supervisor.
3. One worktree/container per agent, with protected branches.
4. Required CI, static analysis, security scans and independent reviewer agents.
5. Harbor plus project-specific regression tasks for pre-release evaluation.
6. OpenTelemetry/OpenInference traces stored in Langfuse or Phoenix.
7. A final human approval bound to a concrete evidence bundle.

That bundle should include the issue/spec, base and resulting commit hashes, diff, commands executed, complete test output, CI links, reviewer findings, unresolved warnings, trace/run ID and approval identity. An agent saying “tests passed” is a claim; immutable logs and CI attestations are evidence.

My short list would therefore be:

- Best autonomous engineering substrate: [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands)
- Best customizable orchestration runtime: [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) or [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen)
- Best explicit AI-software-company models: [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) and [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev)
- Most interesting SDLC-native newcomers: [metaswarm](https://github.com/dsifry/metaswarm), [tutti](https://github.com/nutthouse/tutti), [kandev](https://github.com/kdlbs/kandev) and [Overstory](https://github.com/jayminwest/overstory)
- Best reproducible agent evaluation layer: [Harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor)
- Best trace/evidence layer: [Langfuse](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) or [Phoenix](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix)
